newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Daiwa manager gets two months in prison.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Daiwa manager gets two months in prison.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent
The former general manager of the Daiwa Bank Ltd.'s New York branch was sentenced Friday to two months in prison for helping to conceal $1.1 billion in trading losses from U.S. regulators.

Although a federal probation department recommended that the defendant Masahiro Tsuda receive no prison sentence, U.S. District Judge Sidney Stein said the term was necessary to deter foreign corporations and their employees from breaking U.S. laws.
He said foreign defendants would be encouraged to ignore regulations if they only risked minimal penalities.
"A message must be sent ... United States laws must be complied with," the judge said.

Stein also fined Tsuda $100,000 and ordered him to serve one year of probation in the United States or Japan. Tsuda, 54, must also post a $50,000 security bond to ensure he will return to the United States if he breaks any more laws in this country.

The judge said he was also imposing the prison term because Tsuda was a manager and had asked others, including a senior vice president, to help cover up the losses. Although Tsuda did not orchestrate the scheme, Stein said his role involved more than minimal planning and repeated illegal acts including falsifying records.
However, he said he would not give the maximum prison term because Tsuda had been a "signficant source of information" to the government in its investigation of the scandal.
"He did not attempt to minimise his role to evoke sympathy or curry favour," the judge said.

Tsuda had pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy in April. Although he admitted breaking U.S. laws, he had done so at the behest of his superiors at Daiwa, which is based in Osaka, Japan, and of Japan's Ministry of Finance.
He said he had taken similar actions in the late 1980s to cover up a $30 million trading loss.
The plea agreement provided that prosecutors drop a count of concealing a felony.
"I had an obligation to follow U.S. law and I and others should have done so," Tsuda told Stein. "I want to stress ... how truly sorry I am for any harm I caused the United States and its people."

In February, Daiwa Bank pleaded guilty to charges of concealing the loss and agreed to pay $340 million in fines, the largest criminal fine levied against a financial institution in the United States.

The charges stem from the conduct of its top management during the summer of 1995, when managers deliberately covered up huge trading losses incurred by Toshihide Iguchi, an executive vice president at the New York branch.

Iguchi pleaded guilty to charges of doctoring bank records and embezzlement, stemming from the $1.1 billion in trading losses that he accumulated and covered up over 12 years. He is awaiting sentencing.

Tsuda's lawyer Stanley Arkin asked that his client be spared a prison term because of the cultural differences between Japan and the United States. He said that following orders is much more ingrained in Japanese society than in the United States. He also said that Tsuda and his family would be ostrasized by society because of a prison sentence.
Stein rejected the arguments and said that Tsuda had been "quite clear" about understanding U.S. law and its consequences.
Tsuda said he had learned of the trading losses in a telephone call from Japan on July 25, 1995, less than three weeks after becoming general manager of the branch.

Tsuda said the deputy president of Daiwa had instructed him to assist in an internal probe of the loss and told him the results of the investigation were not to be disclosed until after Sept. 30, the end of Daiwa's fiscal year.
